problem: The rule 'Reject H₀ if |t| exceeds the critical value' is wrong for a one-tailed test. With H₁: μ < 250 g in Worked example 1 and critical value 1.833, a sample giving t = +2.5 (x̄ above 250 g) has |t| = 2.5 > 1.833 and the rule tells the student to reject — a rejection in the direction opposite to the alternative. Taking absolute value also throws away the sign that the chapter itself says must be kept.
fix: Reject H₀ when t falls in the tail named by H₁: reject if t > t(α, df) for H₁: μ > μ₀, or if t < −t(α, df) for H₁: μ < μ₀. Use |t| > t(α/2, df) only for the two-tailed test.

where: Exam traps, third bullet ('Losing the sign')
problem: The advice 'Compare |t| with the two-tailed critical value' describes only a two-tailed test and conflicts with the one-tailed procedure used earlier in the chapter; a student applying it to a one-tailed problem will use the wrong column of the t table.
fix: Say: keep the sign while deciding. For a one-tailed test compare the signed t with the one-tailed critical value; for a two-tailed test compare |t| with t(α/2, df). In both cases read the direction of the effect from the sign of t before writing the conclusion.

where: Section 3 assumptions, last bullet ('Confusing the pooled variance with an average of the variances')
problem: The wording is self-contradictory: the pooled variance is weighted by degrees of freedom n − 1, which is close to the sample size, and then the sentence says 'so a small group counts less' — which is the effect of the sample size. A student can read this as saying the two weightings point in opposite directions.
fix: Write: the pooled value weights each variance by its degrees of freedom, n₁ − 1 and n₂ − 1. A small group therefore contributes little, so it cannot swing the pooled estimate, but a very small group also makes s_p² unreliable.

problem: 'The degrees of freedom come from the branch, not from the sample size alone' is misleading: the degrees of freedom come from the branch and the sample sizes together (n − 1; n₁ + n₂ − 2).
fix: Write: 'Choose the branch from the design of the study; the degrees of freedom then follow from that branch and the sample sizes.' Also add 'df = n₁ + n₂ − 2' to the 'Two independent' note and 'df = n − 1 on the differences' to the 'Paired data' note, so all three branches show their df.
